lead: Charpit's method solves a general first-order PDE F(x, y, z, p, q) = 0 when the standard substitutions of 4.2 do not fit. It finds a second relation between p and q, solves the two relations for p and q, then integrates dz = p dx + q dy. The result is a complete integral with two constants. Engineers use it for nonlinear wave fronts, Hamilton–Jacobi problems in control, and any first-order surface equation that resists fixed tricks.
prereq: You need: 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, partial derivatives, and ordinary integration.

sections.h3: Why a second relation is needed

blocks.text: A first-order PDE in two independent variables x and y has the form F(x, y, z, p, q) = 0. Here z is the unknown surface, p = ∂z/∂x and q = ∂z/∂y. One equation with two unknown functions p and q leaves freedom. A complete integral must carry two arbitrary constants a and b.

blocks.where: z = z(x, y) is the surface; p = ∂z/∂x; q = ∂z/∂y; F is a given smooth function.

blocks.text: Charpit supplies a second equation f(x, y, z, p, q, a) = 0. It is chosen so that F = 0 and f = 0 can be solved for p and q. Then dz = p dx + q dy is integrated to get z = φ(x, y, a, b).

Use Charpit when 4.2 fails: for equations such as p q = z, p² + q² = z, or Clairaut-type z = p x + q y + f(p, q) with nonlinear terms. For linear Pp + Qq = R, Charpit reduces to Lagrange's method (4.3), so use that shorter route.
dx/F_p = dy/F_q = dz/(p F_p + q F_q) = −dp/(F_x + p F_z) = −dq/(F_y + q F_z)
blocks.where: F_p = ∂F/∂p, and similarly F_x, F_y, F_z, F_q; p and q are evaluated from the surface.

blocks.text: Compute five partial derivatives: F_x, F_y, F_z, F_p, F_q. Write the chain. Pick a pair with easy integration. The usual pair is −dp/(F_x + p F_z) = −dq/(F_y + q F_z), or one side with dx or dy. Integrate to get f(...) = a.
Keep the minus signs. They come from the characteristic equations and flip signs when F_z is nonzero. For F = p q − z, F_z = −1, so −dp/(pF_z) = dp/p, not −dp/p.

items: Write F = 0; find F_x, F_y, F_z, F_p, F_q.
Write the chained equalities from the formula.
Integrate one usable pair; name the constant a.
Solve F = 0 and f = a for p and q.
Put p and q into dz = p dx + q dy and integrate; name the new constant b.
Write z = φ(x, y, a, b); verify by substitution.

sections.h3: From p and q to the complete integral

blocks.text: After step 4, p and q contain a and the variables. Substitute them into dz = p dx + q dy. Integrate in two stages: treat y as constant and integrate in x, then add an unknown function of y; differentiate the result with respect to y and match q. In many Charpit problems the variables separate directly, so one integration gives the answer.

Charpit's equations guarantee that the resulting expression is an exact differential, so the integration is path-independent. The final z has two constants a and b. A complete integral is not the general solution; it is a two-parameter family. Selecting constants to fit a curve is the Cauchy problem (4.5).
Check the answer by computing p and q from z and substituting into F. If F is not zero, an integration constant or sign is wrong. For Pfaffian integrability conditions, see 4.6.

figure.caption: Charpit moves from the PDE to a second relation, solves for p and q, then integrates dz to reach a complete integral with two constants.

spec.title: Charpit's method
spec.aria: Flowchart shows Charpit's auxiliary equations giving one integral, then p and q, then integration of dz to a complete integral.

examples.question: Solve p q = z by Charpit's method, and verify the complete integral for a = 4, b = 1 at (x, y) = (0, 0).
steps: Write F = p q − z. Then F_x = 0, F_y = 0, F_z = −1, F_p = q, F_q = p.
Charpit's equations: dx/q = dy/p = dz/(2 p q) = −dp/(0 + p(−1)) = −dq/(0 + q(−1)). The last two simplify to dp/p and dq/q.
From dp/p = dq/q, integrate: ln p = ln q + ln a, so p = a q. Here a > 0 is a constant.
Substitute into F: (a q) q − z = 0, so a q² = z. Hence q = √(z/a) and p = a q = √(a z).
Now dz = p dx + q dy = √(a z) dx + √(z/a) dy. Divide by √z: dz/√z = √a dx + (1/√a) dy.
Integrate: 2√z = √a x + y/√a + c. Multiply by √a: 2√(a z) = a x + y + b, where b = c√a.
Square: 4 a z = (a x + y + b)². This is the complete integral.
examples.answer: The complete integral is 4 a z = (a x + y + b)². With a = 4, b = 1 at (0, 0), z = 0.0625, p = 0.5, q = 0.125, and p q = 0.0625 = z.

traps: Losing the minus signs in −dp and −dq. The denominators are F_x + pF_z and F_y + qF_z, so F_z = −1 changes the sign.
Forgetting F_z in the denominator. For F = p q − z, omitting F_z gives the wrong second relation and the wrong p, q.
Integrating dz = p dx + q dy while p and q still contain symbols. Substitute p and q as functions of x, y, z and a first.
Using only one constant. The first integral contributes a; the integration of dz contributes b. A complete integral needs both.
Dividing by p or q without noting the degenerate case. In p q = z, a = 0 forces p = 0 and z = 0, the trivial surface.

quiz.q: Write Charpit's auxiliary equations for F(x, y, z, p, q) = 0.
quiz.a: dx/F_p = dy/F_q = dz/(pF_p + qF_q) = −dp/(F_x + pF_z) = −dq/(F_y + qF_z).

quiz.q: Why does F = 0 alone not give p and q?
quiz.a: It is one equation in two unknowns p and q. A complete integral needs two constants, so a second compatible relation is required.

quiz.q: Solve p² + q² = 1 by Charpit's method.
quiz.a: F = p² + q² − 1. F_x = F_y = F_z = 0, so dp = 0 and dq = 0. Thus p = a and q = b with a² + b² = 1. Then dz = a dx + b dy, so z = a x + b y + c with b = √(1 − a²). The complete integral is z = a x + √(1 − a²) y + c.

quiz.q: In p q = z, what goes wrong at a = 0?
quiz.a: p = a q gives p = 0. Then F gives z = 0. The solution collapses to the trivial surface z = 0; the family with a > 0 covers nontrivial surfaces.

quiz.q: For F = p q − z, express p and q using a.
quiz.a: p = a q and a q² = z, so q = √(z/a) and p = √(a z).

quiz.q: Why must p and q be substituted before integrating dz = p dx + q dy?
quiz.a: The integrand must contain only x, y, z and constants. Leaving p and q as symbols gives an expression that cannot be integrated as a differential in x and y.
A solution z = φ(x, y, a, b) containing two independent arbitrary constants a and b.

quiz.q: A student writes +dp/(F_x + pF_z). What error follows for F = p q − z?
quiz.a: For F = p q − z, F_z = −1 and F_x = 0. The correct term is −dp/(−p) = dp/p. A wrong overall sign changes the integrated relation between p and q, so the second equation is not compatible with F and the final surface fails substitution.

beyond: Not for the exam. Charpit's equations are the characteristic equations of a first-order PDE, and in Hamilton–Jacobi theory they become Hamiltonian ODEs for action. In optimal control and robotics, the same equations propagate cost-to-go surfaces. In geometric optics they trace wave fronts. Search for 'method of characteristics nonlinear PDE' and 'Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation'.
